sections.title: Woord Vooraf In Memoriam (p.2)
sections.text: FOREWORD In your hands is the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2020. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, and the actions the shore organization took to facilitate these deployments. The year began as in previous years. This changed when, at the end of February and the beginning of March, COVID-19 also affected the Netherlands. Virtually the entire society came to a standstill, and the Royal Netherlands Navy had to adapt significantly. The lockdowns and safety regulations had a major impact on the workplace. The departments and units improvised and quickly regrouped so that the organization could function properly. In a safe manner, personnel followed many new courses, training sessions, and participated in (international) exercises. This was done differently than usual; sometimes from home, or in the workplace at a distance of one and a half meters. We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy. Foreword Commander of the Naval Forces Vice Admiral Rob Kramer.

sections.text: 19 Organizational overviews shock-resistant budget. The expenditures by CZSK (Article 2 of the defense budget) were higher in 2020 than initially allocated at the beginning of the year. Compared to the draft budget, more was realized in readiness. The main reason is the usual interdepartmental transfer from the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management for payments to the Rijksrederij by the Coast Guard Netherlands for buoying tasks and emergency towing assistance. Within the maintenance category, various increases occurred throughout the year, leading to higher expenditures. This was partly due to the year-end margin of 2019, higher VAT receipts, various reallocations within the navy to reduce the deficit in maintenance, and several other mutations (€5.6 million). The under-realization elsewhere in the budget was also utilized for expenditures on the maintenance process. In personnel expenditures, more was spent overall than indicated in the draft budget. The cause lies mainly in additional expenditures on pension premiums from Article 10, higher employer costs, and labor conditions. On the other hand, less was spent due to the effects of COVID-19 on activity-related allowances, training, business trips, other personal expenses, and budget was made available for maintenance issues. Luyckx The Directorate Personnel and Organization is the supporting directorate within CZSK regarding personnel, training, healthcare, and organization. DP&O is the directorate that, within its scope and resources, ensures that the personnel of the Royal Netherlands Navy have every opportunity to further develop and grow and adequately responds to those matters in the environment that can contribute to good employment practices. For 2020, the focal points of the directorate were: Further developing personnel framework plans. Ensuring that inspiring Professionally Oriented Education (BGO) takes place within CZSK by modernizing training with the use of modern learning tools, innovation, and establishing a connection between the operational and training domains. Applying management on operational personnel needs. Optimizing recruitment of civilian personnel. Supporting the Directorate Personnel's policy plan on Diversity & Inclusion. Intensifying the Personnel and Organization (P&O) approach with a positive effect on retention. Applying the developed Career Paths for medical personnel. Legal Affairs (JUZA) Head: Commander (cdr) G. Souer, LLD The JUZA department is part of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DP&O), one of the five line directorates of the CZSK. The department advises and supports the CZSK, the directors of the CZSK, and unit commanders on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within the CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within the CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and constitutional and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different offices. Thus, every employee at JUZA can serve as the first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department. JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of the CZSK and the Ministry of Defence as an organization. Should a military member be involved in a criminal case, they can receive assistance from the Ministry of Defence in this matter. Personnel and Organization (P&O) Head: Captain (ktz) E.C.W. Jansen General Last year saw significant changes in the P&O domain. To retain more personnel for the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM), efforts were made to focus more on the individual. Additionally, COVID-19 had a considerable impact, and employees often worked 'remotely' and from home. Many changes had already been initiated, funded by the Second Chamber Motion Van der Staaij, further development of the armed forces (DOKM), and defense-wide projects such as Retention and Recruitment. Various measures that were implemented have now been secured in operations. For instance, an Oceangoing Patrol Vessel (OPV) remained in the Caribbean and was manned with a relief crew (the so-called multiple-crewing concept).

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.4)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-4 23 Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Bi-national Support Team (BST) Multipurpose Frigates received further development this year. Many organizational parts grew, either from the Van der Staaij motion or DOKM measures (temporary or not), as well as from strengthening the security chain. Furthermore, the measures from the Labor Conditions Agreement 18-20 were translated into regulations, from which HR measures followed. Part of this was the new Human Resources (HR) model developed by the Directorate of Personnel. The new model was intended to provide more opportunities for flexibility and customization for agreements between employees and supervisors. In fulfilling positions, the needs of the organization and the talents of employees in relation to the organization were better mapped and combined. New appointment and contract forms, strategic talent management, and the remuneration model are topics in the new HR model that affect the legal status of employees. A pilot environment at the Submarine Service has started to test some of these topics for feasibility. The Royal Netherlands Navy continued to face a significant personnel shortage this year. Measures to promote personnel retention were articulated in fourteen Personnel measures, drafted in September 2019 by the AR. The implementation of these measures received much attention alongside regular work. The measure to develop and implement a new HR system for CZSK was the most impactful. The old job allocation process was no longer functioning and needed to be simplified. To this end, a research study was conducted last year that will be further developed in 2021. It was investigated whether the Royal Fleet Auxiliary concept is applicable to a Hydrographic Survey Vessel (HOV), and the possibilities of 'alternative manning' for Combat Support Ships were mapped. The job vacancy bank was cleaned up to improve its functionality and transparency. Furthermore, it has been incorporated into operations that military personnel working at CZSK will be assessed once in their position. This could contribute to personnel retention, allowing for better alignment with the long-term objectives and development needs of military personnel. Units of the OPE fleet are manned task-oriented (warfare), with a guaranteed minimum staffing of CoCe. The effect is that high-end warfare, single threat can be secured, and not always multi-threat. In the career guidance section, starting qualifications (MBO3 level) have been established for the sub-service groups Logistics Service and Marines. Pul Head of Integrated Security Staff Office: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) P.B.A. Coster In 2012, the three-director model was introduced within Defense. This was the result of the defense-wide reorganization following the measures from the defense memorandum “Defense after the Credit Crisis, a Smaller Armed Forces in an Unstable World” (April 8, 2011). This reorganization was carried out based on pressing financial, personnel, and organizational frameworks. Based on this, it was decided at that time to divide staff, operational, and governance tasks of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) among the directors of Personnel and Operations and Material Maintenance, with the P-CZSK expected to fulfill the central coordinating role. In practice, it soon became clear that this organizational investment brought structural shortcomings in the areas of governance integrity, span/scope of control, allocation of responsibilities, oversight, and the absence of escalation levels. Furthermore, attention to personnel, operations, governance risks, and oversight increased significantly, and the intensity of governance coordination between internal and external interfaces grew. To achieve more balance in the governance organization of the CZSK, clarity in ownership, and in operations, C-ZSK requested the Chief of Defense Staff (CDS) to agree to the expansion of the framework of the three-director model. This provided the opportunity to establish a new directorate under a single leadership,

This year, these specialized units worked with both the snowmobile and the BV-206 tracked vehicles. From a new base location in Skjold, 2MCG, supplemented by units from the German Seebatallion and the Belgian Special Operations Regiment, completed a challenging training in extreme terrain since early January. About 470 marines, including 154 novices, completed a physically and mentally challenging program in which units were trained to successfully conduct operations in Military Operations in eXtreme conditions (MOX) terrain. Operating under extreme climatic and geographical conditions requires specific knowledge, skills, and experience to perform under these circumstances and to be independently deployable for longer durations. sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2020_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-36 95 The Operations Directorate's personal interaction and information exchange were significantly impacted by the pandemic. Restrictions on the number of personnel in the building and at the workplace, limits on the size and frequency of meetings, conferences, and working groups, and the closing of various international borders led to the necessity of quickly seeking alternative ways to remain effective. Fortunately, JIVC was able to rapidly roll out Skype and Ms-Teams for low classified virtual meetings, allowing everyone to increasingly communicate; in civilian attire from their kitchen tables. For the higher classified meetings, it was more complicated to get them off the ground. As a result, several valuable international contacts were at risk of being lost. The leadership of the MWC primarily focused on keeping the crew engaged with the organization, despite them being partially 'unwelcome' at the workplace. It was striking to see how the annually recurring meetings became increasingly limited in size and setting. Of the large meetings, the NATO Maritime Operations Working Group in Albania still took place more or less normally, but the Amphibious Operations Work Group was a virtual meeting. The Steering Group Meetings of the maritime COEs could take place in Ostend, Norfolk, and Kiel due to a temporary easing of the restrictions. However, various conferences, seminars, and working groups dwindled, were postponed, or were organized virtually (if possible). The Maritime Battle Lab remained very active despite all COVID restrictions and conducted activities for the MTMD forum, Spartan Windmill 3, Ship in the Loop test, Augmented Reality Tests, and Connectivity tests with the F-35. the role of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean region. The Command of the Navy in the Caribbean is responsible for maritime security, law enforcement, and disaster relief operations. The operational area is characterized by various factors such as the significant distance from the Netherlands, a large maritime accountability area, tropical climatic conditions, numerous direct political and international contacts, and culturally locally determined circumstances. 

Additionally, we observe three developments in the environment in which CZMCARIB operates that significantly influence our actions. Firstly, there is geopolitical destabilization in the region, particularly due to developments in Venezuela. A second development relates to the situation in Venezuela and concerns the increasing influence of criminal organizations. The country is in a humanitarian and economic crisis, resulting in an increase in migration of undocumented individuals and smuggling of contraband such as drugs and weapons. Finally, we see an increase in climatic extremes as a result of global warming. Whether CZMCARIB can adequately fulfill the three main defense tasks with its current capabilities is a legitimate question. In light of the above developments, the Advisory Council on International Affairs, at the request of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, is conducting a study on the role of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean region.

Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of CZSK and translates to the environment in the West as: "Providing security in the Caribbean." This one sentence articulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at the strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of defense in the Caribbean: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.4)
sections.text:
The Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean states that through our presence and our activities, we have a deterrent effect against potential hostilities from foreign countries or organizations. Promoting the international rule of law and stability is part of our second main task, which also includes the deployment for international law enforcement, such as combating the smuggling of weapons and drugs by sea. CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, conducting counter illicit trafficking operations and through international military cooperation. The United States and France are the main international partners in this regard. C-ZMCARIB fulfills the CIT task as Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4), a subordinate commander of the American Joint Interagency Task Force South. It supports civil authorities. The Dutch Armed Forces have developed into a structural security partner within the Kingdom. With its highly developed specialized and unique capabilities, the armed forces now have broader support options. CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB also provides support to third parties, primarily to the Coast Guard in the Caribbean (KWCARIB). C-ZMCARIB is also the Director of KWCARIB. It also provides emergency assistance in disasters and crises. Finally, CZMCARIB also supports the Social Development Programs in Curaçao and Aruba. 

International Drug Enforcement
In addition to the territorial defense of the six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in upholding the international rule of law in the Caribbean. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The navy in the Caribbean is closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South based in Key West. The Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Task Group 4.4, one of the task groups of this organization.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.5)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Vision In order to realize the mission of CZMCARIB as adequately as possible in light of the changes around it, a vision has been established. The vision of CZMCARIB is: ‘CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK.’ This means that CZMCARIB aims to be recognized as the obvious and reliable partner when it comes to contributing to security in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. ‘Relevant maritime’ and ‘security partner’ in the above vision refers to the fact that CZMCARIB assigns a high priority to the second and third core tasks. Due to national and international agreements, it wants to promote the international and local rule of law with its own resources, for example by contributing capabilities to (inter)national organizations or by providing military assistance. With these own resources, it can be deployed for a wide range of scenarios to support civil authorities, for instance for conducting searches, tracking, diving units, observation, and emergency assistance. CZMCARIB does this in good cooperation with national and international partners in the security chain. CZMCARIB also carries out the first core task. Through its forward presence, it fulfills a threshold function with its own personnel and resources. In 2020, Advanced Search Teams and the Explosive Ordnance Disposal Service continued six-week rotations, linked to CIDW. The Containment of Disturbances Platoon regularly conducted integration training/exercises with the Curaçao Police Corps (KPC) and/or the Curaçao Volunteer Corps with support from instructors of the Royal Marechaussee.

sections.text: 7_Navy_Annual_Report_2020_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-9 132 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean The MSC permanently supported the SSCG with boarding capacity. The annual large-scale exercise of the MSC, exercise Caribbean Urban Warrior in the United States (Camp LeJeune) in March, unfortunately had to be canceled halfway through the training due to COVID-19. Military assistance from CZMCARIB provided soft and hard military support in 64 cases to the authorities of the countries and islands of the Kingdom. Some examples are described below: In the period from May to June, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman and embarked forces provided support in the Caribbean in the context of the COVID-19 crisis. From April 27 to June 15, 107 Asbt from the Royal Netherlands Army Command supported from Aruba with the X-300, a UAV, in order to map possible illegal influx from South America. On almost all islands within the Kingdom, engineers assisted with searches of prisons, homes, properties, and vehicles. Among other things, phones, money, drugs, and documents were found. Curaçao Militia (CURMIL), MSC, and CIDW provided hard military assistance during large-scale unrest in Curaçao in July. The CURMIL, MSC, and CIDW established long-term static observation posts offloading Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman near Philipsburg.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.10)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Curaçao and Aruba in support of KWCARIB, focusing on illegal landings due to the deteriorating (COVID-19) situation in Venezuela. In Curaçao, assistance was provided multiple times to security partners through diving capacity. In Curaçao and Sint Maarten, hard military assistance was provided in enforcing COVID-19 measures, including enforcing the curfew. Soft military assistance was provided by, among other things, parking CUROIL vehicles at Marinekazerne Suffisant in connection with the unrest in Curaçao related to the refinery. Support was given to the fire department in Curaçao by destroying seized and/or surrendered flares by the EODD. A safe house was established at Marinebasis Parera to support the Curaçao Police Corps during the visit of the State Secretary for the Interior during his visit to Curaçao from September 1 to 3. On September 21, a diving accident occurred in the dry dock of Damen Shiprepair Curaçao. CZMCARIB provided support at the request of the Public Prosecution Service in Curaçao in investigating the circumstances of the accident by making the CARIB diving team available. The Caribbean militias reinforced the duty teams of KWCARIB starting in March to increase the sailing capacity of KWCARIB. The FRISC troop also supported KWCARIB multiple times with FRISCs and crews. Visiting units Throughout 2020, several units from the Netherlands came to Curaçao and Aruba to conduct their training there. Due to the COVID-19 outbreak, the majority of training was canceled starting in March. Directorate Control Head: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) ing. P. Borsje-Senders The staff department of Directorate Control consists of the F&C office and the Management Information office and is formally under F&C CZSK. The objective of Directorate Control is to support C-ZMCARIB in the preparation, execution, progress, and quality of financial policy advising. They also assist in compiling the budget, establishing the spending program, and providing information through management and steering reports.

sections.text: 7_Navy_Annual_Report_2020_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-11 134 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Marine Base Parera (MBPAR) Commander (kltz) R.A.J. Wesdorp MSc The motto accompanying the emblem of MBPAR is 'cheerful and bold'. Two character traits that are characteristic of a good 'host'. The base houses the staff of C-ZMCARIB and the Search and Coordination Center of the Coast Guard Caribbean Area. MBPAR also provides accommodation for a rotating company of the army. They are initially in the Caribbean for a training program. If necessary, they also provide humanitarian assistance, for example after a hurricane or to maintain public order. The company is also deployed for ceremonial tasks, such as at the Opening of the States. This boat group at MBPAR is primarily used to support various operations and exercises. In addition, they can also conduct beach reconnaissance and river operations. The Navy Operations Center is also located at Marine Base Parera. This center directs all counter-drug operations in the Caribbean. The base has workshops where all sailing and rolling equipment is maintained. Anaconda vehicles at Marine Base Parera.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.12)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean During the pandemic, the GGD opened a testing facility at the base. COVID-19 meant that certain maintenance tasks could not be carried out. For example, the replacement of the ICT cabling in the buildings on the staff hill did not take place. However, the deployment of Securitas to improve access control at the gates was able to continue. Marine Barracks Suffisant (MKSUF) Commander: Major (majmarns) C. van Dinteren, from August 27 Major (majmarns) S. Baan Like the rest of the Kingdom, 2020 was entirely focused on COVID-19, yet the barracks continued to operate without interruption. In fact, due to the pandemic, the demand for additional enforcement capacity in Curaçao was greater than ever before. This led to improved collaborations with local authorities (notably the KPC) and strengthened the position of the CURMIL. The deployment of local military personnel in enforcing the curfew, combating unrest in downtown Willemstad, and addressing whale threats was successful. After years of efforts to professionalize the CURMIL, MKSUF (particularly the CURMIL) could count on the respect of the local population as well as that of local authorities such as the KPC in 2020. The long-term professionalization of the CURMIL characterized internal operations through inventiveness and flexibility, with barracks personnel making significant contributions. Without a substantial budget, the results this year were visible through the deployment of CURMIL as an operational unit. On August 27, Major (majmarns) C. van Dinteren, who remained involved in this role until the last day despite a serious illness, handed over command to Major (majmarns) S. Baan. Marine Barracks Savaneta Aruba (MSKSAV) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) B. van Beekhuizen Marine Barracks Savaneta is located in Aruba and houses the 32RSQN and the Aruban Militia. These consist of a staff, platoons, and supporting units. The marine squadron and the Aruban Militia (ARUMIL) have various tasks. For this, they train and exercise in the United States, French Guiana, Suriname, French Caribbean islands, and the Windward and Leeward Islands. A platoon of the Aruban militia guards and secures the barracks.

Noordam after a term of four years. Additionally, the new position of Head of Staff was created following the reorganization in August of this year. Relationships were strengthened over the past year with the Emergency Operation Center (EOC) with representatives from various ministries. The detachment actively contributed to intensifying relationships within the EOC, including support for a Table Top training for disaster preparedness. Relationships were also strengthened within Emergency Support Function 5, the body that represents all safety partners in Sint Maarten. At least once a quarter, the EOC and Emergency Support Function 5 team now meet to discuss what the needs are. Military Assistance The detachment provided three months of military assistance in support of COVID-19 lockdown enforcement. During the 2020 hurricane season, the detachment provided military assistance at the request of the government of Sint Maarten in close cooperation with the Sint Maarten Police Corps during Tropical Storm Isaias. Fortunately, the damage was limited. The team also supported in October with military search capacity at the prison, resulting in various seizures. Raiding Section With the start of the team in August, it managed, despite all the COVID-related issues, to ensure that the weapons were zeroed and that the drivers of the Anaconda vehicles were able to obtain their licenses. This was the main priority for the unit. Subsequently, several exercises took place in Sint Maarten to assess the team's level and practice skills in preparation for the following year. Events Due to COVID-19, the barracks unfortunately could not organize a Marine run and Beat the Marines with support from the Physical Training & Sports office from Curaçao.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.14)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Infrastructure The RS has settled at the secondary location Gonzalo, which consists of three residential towers. Two of the residential towers have been adapted to serve as training locations but also for the storage of personal equipment. The third residential tower provides space to accommodate onboard personnel (military members who not only work at the barracks but also live there) and potentially house small self-supporting units. Since there is now a permanent element, marines are offered the opportunity to be stationed for two years, with most renting a house on the island. Due to the further postponement of the planned construction of the new support base until 2026, various repairs and/or adjustments took place. This was to ensure that the personnel can still make use of the temporary housing at Point Blanche until the transition to the new construction. The port company addressed various leaks, and a thorough repainting took place, making the MSTPPB look fresh again. Personnel of the Marine Support Point Point Blanche.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.15)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Support Vessel Zr.Ms. Pelikaan Commander: Lt. D.M. Boom The year began for Zr.Ms. Pelikaan differently than any other year. The ship was not in Curaçao after more than ten years, but in the Netherlands for the Midlife Update (MLU). In the first months, everything went smoothly. The maintenance progressed steadily, and the crew regularly returned home to Curaçao in small groups to keep work and home life in balance. Unfortunately, starting in March, things changed from what was planned. Due to COVID-19, Curaçao went into lockdown. The crew that was in Curaçao could not return to the Netherlands and vice versa. Fortunately, the Netherlands did not go (completely) into lockdown, and all maintenance work on the ship could continue as planned. The crew worked hard on the renewed ship, and it paid off. What followed were the sailing material tests and seaworthiness tests. For the crew, it was mainly getting used to working with the newly installed much larger crane. After this, the signal was given to start the workup. With many new personnel, the learning curve for SARC 3 was steep, but the crew also overcame this hurdle. On September 17, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan departed towards the sea to Curaçao. The ship Zr.Ms. Pelikaan at the dock at Damen Shipyard for a Midlife Update.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.16)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean maneuvered steadily between all hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean and arrived, ahead of schedule, in Willemstad on October 1. At a proper COVID-19 distance, the vessel was warmly welcomed. Transport between the islands had, of course, been at a standstill for some time. Therefore, the familiar trips to Aruba and Sint Maarten followed. The boat group practiced to reacquaint everyone with the platform and the changes that the crane had brought. Finally, at the end of the year, a voyage to Bonaire took place for various inspections that needed to be conducted on Dutch territory. Fortunately, COVID-19 had been somewhat contained, and the crew was able to enjoy a short port visit, of course with the necessary PCR tests beforehand. sections.text: Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied Medical Service CZMCARIB Head: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) M.G.J. van der Aa The Primary Health Care Company (EGB) and the Defence Dental Service provide primary care in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom from the Health Centre Curaçao. Additionally, there is a branch at the location Aruba. At both centres, they provide integrated care to military personnel and deployed Dutch civilian staff. Furthermore, the Dental Service and EGB in the CARIB offer 24/7 care to the accompanying family members of the deployed staff. The personnel of the EGB also provide operational support to the MHKC. In 2020, the care provided by EGB CUR was primarily focused on COVID-19. The support that had been provided to the local Public Health Service (GGD) since July 2019 continued in 2020 (setting up GGD testing sites, assisting with contact tracing among their own personnel, and opening their own COVID-19 testing site at MBPAR). They also provided daily care to personnel who tested positive and were placed in quarantine at MKSUF. This support was ongoing throughout the year. In addition to all COVID-19 care, the EGB made every effort to continue daily care. Training and exercises also continued, often medically supported by the EGB. As a result, operational readiness was guaranteed. A work agreement was signed with the local ambulance service, Fundacion Kuido Di Ambulans Korsou, on September 18. By appointment, they ensure the availability of a civilian ambulance at the training area Wacawa. This provides broader medical support for shooting training there. With some adjustments in logistics and general procedures, customer support at the locations Curaçao and Aruba was well secured. However, travel to Sint Maarten and Bonaire was not possible.

sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean The Coast Guard collaborates with the Royal Marechaussee on patrols around Aruba. A project group has been established with various suppliers to improve the identified bottlenecks. In 2021, the Coast Guard will implement the recommendations of the project group. The shore radar detection system consists of a complete set of sensors, connections, and software. This system ultimately ensures total radar detection capacity over the Windward Islands. Due to the aging of the systems and travel restrictions related to COVID-19, it has proven very difficult to have the current chain perform to standard in 2020. Throughout the year, various malfunctions occurred on all islands. These were partly caused by the climbability of the masts, a crucial factor in safely carrying out maintenance, not always being guaranteed. For this reason, the Coast Guard invested in 2020 in a minimal solution to keep the masts safely and independently climbable until their replacement takes place in 2021. The average material availability across all eight radar locations in 2020 was 80%, compared to the standard of 95%. sections.text: On March 9, the traditional KVMO-Winnubst concert took place at the KIM. The traditional concert of the KVMO, supported by the Winnubst harmony orchestra from Den Helder, once again connected the people of Den Helder with the KIM and thus also with the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM). Winnubst showcased its best side, and the hospitality of the KVMO and the KIM was also on display. With vocal support from Karen Klopstra and Marit Tesselaar and various musical soloists, the small hall of the KIM was more than filled. Then, in mid-March 2020, the cabinet announced the first general measures to combat COVID-19, and the Netherlands went into partial lockdown. At the KIM, the instructors sent the cadets home, and lessons took place online as much as possible. With the guidelines from the RIVM in mind, contact education could resume in early May, and after a quarantine period, sailing resumed with the training vessel MOV Van Kinsbergen and Zr.Ms. Urania. Nevertheless, in this exceptional pandemic year, it proved possible to welcome a group of approximately 100 aspiring cadets at the KIM. During the maritime introduction period (after the quarantine weeks), the future leaders learned how to act as team players within the armed forces in general and specifically within the KM. On Texel, the focus was on basic military training and pushing physical limits. This was followed by a sailing period aboard the Norwegian three-masted sailing ship Statsraad Lehmkuhl. Here, the aspiring cadets became acquainted with the sea and the elements. In addition, they learned how to safely perform seamanship tasks aboard a ship. The Maritime Introduction Period (MIP) formed the first part of the training curriculum at the KIM. This curriculum focused on competencies such as decisiveness, teamwork, communication, stress resilience, and sense of responsibility. Leadership is the common thread throughout the training. The aspirants are expected to ultimately be able to lead, guide, support, and delegate. This professional training is an essential part of the officer training program. Therefore, despite the ongoing pandemic, it was decided to carry out the MIP as fully as possible. To do this responsibly, the KIM implemented risk-mitigating measures, including a two-week quarantine period.
